Sarah Game's bill restricting late-term abortions has progressed to the lower house.  (ABC News: Che Chorley)

A bill to restrict late-term abortions has been defeated in SA Parliament's lower house, 36 votes to 9.

The legislation would have restricted access to abortion after 25 weeks, and had passed the parliament's upper house earlier on Wednesday.

South Australia’s lower house has voted down a bill to restrict access to late-term abortion, after the legislation had earlier passed the upper house.

The bill was defeated 36 votes to 9 shortly after 9:30pm ACST, following less than two hours of debate.

Only 12 of the 47 MPs in the lower house spoke on the bill.

Both premier Peter Malinauskas and opposition leader Ashton Hurn voted in favour of the bill, but did not speak.

The matter was a conscience vote for Labor and Liberal MPs. The Greens voted against it, while One Nation supported it.

Earlier, one Labor source told the ABC there was "nervous optimism" the bill would be voted down in the lower house.

Sarah Game announces her move to Family First at South Australia's Parliament House alongside national director Lyle Shelton. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The bill, introduced by Family First MP Sarah Game in the upper house, would have effectively banned abortion from 25 weeks onwards except when necessary to save the life of the mother or in cases of serious fetal abnormalities.

The original bill precluded fetal abnormalities as a reason for access to a late-term abortion, however the exemption was later included after an amendment by Labor MP Tung Ngo.

Mr Ngo said he did not support late-term abortion but was "against forcing families into suffering when the medical reality is clear and the outcome is heartbreak".

Labor MP Tung Ngo added an amendment to Ms Game's bill. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"We trust families every day with decisions about life and death, we trust them because they are the ones that love that person most," he said.

Earlier on Wednesday, Ms Game's bill passed the upper house 10 votes to 9 with the support of three newly-elected One Nation MPs.

It is the furthest an anti-abortion bill has made it through South Australia’s parliament, after two earlier bids in 2024 and 2025 were voted down by the upper house.

South Australian law permits abortions after 23 weeks, with the approval of two doctors, if the continuation of the pregnancy would involve "significant risk of injury to the physical or mental health" of the pregnant person.

This bill would have removed that exemption.

The government indicated on Wednesday morning that it would bring the bill to a vote that night if it passed the upper house.

One Nation MP Chantelle Thomas, who introduced the bill in the lower house, unsuccessfully sought to defer the debate until November 25.

She was told by Speaker Nat Cook that the house had agreed to debate the legislation that night.

Ms Thomas criticised the government for the "rushed nature of this vote put on by the government".

"This is a matter on which members should rightly be afforded a conscience vote and as much time as possible to consider it," she said.

"It is disappointing that the members, some new and some old, will now not be able to consult properly with the constituents before speaking for them — especially on such an issue that weighs heavily on many South Australians."

One Nation MP Chantelle Thomas criticised the government for holding the lower house vote immediately after it passed the upper house. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Labor frontbencher Tom Koutsantonis, who supported the bill, accused Ms Thomas of being "misinformed".

"Don't walk in here, 90 days after being elected, and lecture me about conscience votes and lecture me about abortion and lecture me about euthanasia — how dare you.

"I've been doing this for 28 years — you walk in here and disparage my colleagues who are voting on their conscience.

"These are all good people, every member in this place, all of them will be voting their conscience either for or against the bill. None of them with malice, none of them with ideology."

Labor MP and Health Minister Blair Boyer said he opposed the bill both as a matter of conscience and on the advice of medical professionals.

Health Minister Blair Boyer said he supported the right to access abortion as healthcare.  (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

"I am firmly of the belief that we already have a fit for purpose legislative framework that treats abortion as healthcare," he said.

"It was very hard fought and won by people who bravely stood in this place and voted for it and stood on the shoulders of people who bravely called for it from outside this parliament for many many years."

One Nation MLC David Paton supported the bill but said he did not think it was a "black and white subject".

"I am the grandson of a single, young female who if was put in that position today because of abortion laws probably would have made a different decision to what she did almost 70 years ago," he said.

Only three lower house Labor MPs — Mr Malinauskas, Mr Koutsantonis and Michael Brown — supported the legislation. From the Liberal Party, Ms Hurn and Sam Telfer voted in support.

Ms Game's said the make-up of parliament had changed following the state election. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Speaking on the floor of parliament before it was defeated in the lower house, Ms Game said she believed there was support for the bill following the March election result.

"The public's been fully aware of the new parties that have entered this chamber and their stance on abortion."

Greens MLC Melanie Selwood said she was "shocked and appalled" to be debating the bill again.

"I would much rather be here talking about safe and equitable access to abortion," Ms Selwood said.

"But instead, I'm having to defend fundamental healthcare."

Labor upper house MP Russel Wortley called on lower house MPs to vote against the legislation.

"We fought the battle twice and we won it. I would now implore members of the lower house to respect the rights of women to make their decision," he said.

Anti-abortion activist Joanna Howe and Family First MLC Sarah Game attended a rally in support of the late-term abortion bill.  (ABC News: Che Chorley)
